records.text: 119. The Special Rapporteur urges the United Nations country team, including the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the United Nations Development Programme, the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS and the World Health Organization, to continue engaging with relevant States, donors and suppliers to support Cuba in procuring medical equipment, spare parts, consumables, reagents, quality medicines, raw materials and sanitary goods necessary to ensure the highest attainable standard of health. 120. The Special Rapporteur invites UNICEF, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization and the Committee on the Rights of the Child to address issues related to access by Cuban nationals to information, teaching materials and platforms necessary for education, research, development, and academic, cultural, and professional cooperation. She calls on the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, United Nations treaty bodies, the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs and other relevant United Nations entities and mechanisms to work together with the Special Rapporteur in exploring avenues for compensation and redress for victims of human rights violations resulting from unilateral coercive measures

records.text: 118. The Special Rapporteur calls on other special procedure mandate holders to pay due attention to the impact of unilateral coercive measures against Cuba on the population, particularly on the most vulnerable groups.

records.text: 115. The Special Rapporteur welcomes the reports of cooperation of the Government of Cuba with the United Nations country team and specialized entities present in Cuba that work in the humanitarian field and calls on the Government to further strengthen cooperation with United Nations entities, including through the organization of visits by relevant special procedure mandate holders in accordance with established standards for country visits. 116. The Special Rapporteur encourages the Government of Cuba to assess and document the humanitarian impact of unilateral coercive measures imposed by the United States, including through the use of the sanctions monitoring tool developed under the mandate. The collection of factual data, including identifiable causal links, patterns and testimonies, may contribute to the verification of facts and support efforts to ensure access to effective remedies and accountability. 117. The Special Rapporteur calls on the Government of Cuba to make more active use of international mechanisms, processes and bodies, including international adjudication, United Nations entities, the universal periodic review, the monitoring of the Sustainable Development Goals, United Nations human rights treaty bodies and the World Health Organization, to address the negative impact and illegality of unilateral coercive measures imposed against Cuba.

records.text: 106. The Special Rapporteur urges the United States to refrain from using sanctions rhetoric, maximum pressure campaigns, the designation of Cuba as a State sponsor of terrorism and claims concerning the use of forced labour as political instruments or as means to obtain economic advantages or to isolate Cuba from international cooperation, the international financial system or economic resources. She calls on the United States to engage in dialogue to settle disputes in accordance with the principles and norms of international law, bilaterally or through United Nations mechanisms, the World Trade Organization or other relevant international institutions, while assessing, mitigating and monitoring the humanitarian impact of the above-mentioned actions. 107. The Special Rapporteur calls on the United States to lift or suspend all unilateral coercive measures applied to Cuba and Cuban companies, including: the 10 per cent de minimis rule; the exercise of jurisdiction based on payments in United States dollars; restrictions preventing vessels from entering United States ports for 180 days after docking in Cuban ports; and threats to revoke visas or Electronic System for Travel Authorization eligibility. Measures taken to enforce unilateral sanctions against Cuba, including fines imposed on banks, should also be lifted. 108. The Special Rapporteur urges the United States to terminate the state of national emergency in relation to Cuba, as it does not appear to be consistent with article 4 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and to align its national legislation with international law, including international human rights law and the law of international responsibility. 109. Noting that existing general licences related to the delivery of food, medicine and telecommunication services are reportedly insufficient and ineffective, the Special Rapporteur urges the United States to lift all limitations that impede the delivery of essential goods, including food, medicine and medical equipment, and the maintenance and development of critical infrastructure, including water and sanitation systems, construction, electricity supply systems, information and communications technology infrastructure and transportation networks. 110. The Special Rapporteur calls on the United States to repeal legislation threatening to revoke the visas of officials from countries participating in the Cuban medical assistance programme, as such measures may be inconsistent with the principles of sovereign equality and of non-intervention in the domestic affairs of States, with the diplomatic immunities of State officials and with humanitarian principles. 111. The Special Rapporteur calls on the United States to ensure that Cuban nationals have access to information and the use of online platforms, tools and databases in conformity with the right of access to information, the right to education and the right of everyone to benefit from the results of scientific research, as well as academic, sports and cultural cooperation. 112. The Special Rapporteur urges the United States to remove any impediments to the transfer of remittances from abroad to Cuban families, including through Western Union and similar financial service providers. She further calls on banks and private companies, particularly those holding monopolistic positions in the production of relevant goods, to act in accordance with the Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and the guiding principles on sanctions, business and human rights, in order to avoid overcompliance and the resulting violations of the rights of nationals and residents of Cuba, in particular with regard to the delivery of medical equipment and related spare parts, medicines and raw materials for pharmaceutical production, and also goods required for the maintenance of critical infrastructure. 113. The Special Rapporteur urges the United States to fully apply the guiding principles for humanitarian assistance set out in the annex of General Assembly resolution 46/182 to ensure that Cuba has unimpeded access to humanitarian goods, in order to protect lives and ensure the proper functioning of critical infrastructure, and to take due account of the guiding principles on humanitarian action in the unilateral sanctions environment.

records.text: 89. Primary unilateral sanctions and the means of their enforcement, de-risking policies and overcompliance have been substantially exacerbating the humanitarian situation in Cuba, which has already been affected by the economic crisis, natural disasters, the COVID-19 pandemic and other challenges at the national level, and have been designed to prevent Cuba from receiving any economic revenue, especially in hard currency. 90. Restrictions on transactions carried out with Cuba, both offline and online, especially those conducted in United States dollars, the designation of Cuban and third State banks, hotels, tourist agencies, industrial companies, aircraft and vessels, on lists, and the prohibition on vessels entering United States ports for 180 days after visiting Cuban ports, are all aimed at cutting Cuba off from sources of income. They have resulted in a critical decline in the State revenue, hyperinflation, growing poverty and insufficient resources to guarantee the basic needs of population, with a particularly devastating impact on vulnerable groups. 91. Threats to revoke visas or to exclude nationals of countries eligible for the Visa Waiver Program (41 countries as of 2025) from the Electronic System for Travel Authorization, and the measures taken to prevent Cuba from participating in, and benefiting from, international financial institutions and other international organizations are aimed at excluding Cuba from international cooperation, including South-South cooperation, in different areas. 92. Expansion of the United States jurisdiction on the grounds of payment in United States dollars or the use or trade of goods in which 10 or more per cent of the content, technology or patents originated in the United States or is linked to United States companies or persons has no basis in international law. As legal and natural persons in the United States control manufacturing in many high tech areas, and given that such persons have recently acquired suppliers that have traditionally served Cuba, Cuba is unable to sustain the functioning of critical sectors of the economy, including with regard to healthcare, energy production, water supply, food production and preservation, information and communications infrastructure, the manufacturing of basic goods and the provision of other basic services. 93. The unavailability of spare parts, software, operational codes and reparation and maintenance services for existing equipment in the healthcare, energy, water supply, industrial, transportation and other sectors, as well as requests to control who the end user of supplies are, force Cubans to seek alternative types of equipment that contain less than 10 per cent United States-origin components or patents. They are also sometimes required to pay in advance, in full and in hard currency for new equipment, at 35 to 40 per cent above the market price, without any certainty as to whether spare parts, consumables and software for the new equipment will be available in the future. 94. The above measures have prevented Cuba from having the resources to develop and maintain essential infrastructure, including in the areas of health (hospitals), education (schools), housing, transportation, electricity and water supply and civil aviation, and to maintain the level of readiness necessary to respond to natural disasters. The measures have also resulted in the reduction of social support programmes and prevented the implementation of academic, cultural, sport and development projects. They have affected the rights to food, to freedom from poverty, to a decent life and to health, economic, social and cultural rights, the right to development and the achievement of relevant Sustainable Development Goals. 95. The extraterritorial impact of sanctions and sanctions enforcement measures imposed against other States, including the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, further limits the ability of Cuba to procure essential goods, including fuel, to ensure the adequate functioning of critical infrastructure. 96. The measures have resulted in challenges – exacerbated by de-risking policies and overcompliance – with regard to financial transactions. Transferring and receiving money, for example remittances from relatives who are abroad, is hampered for many, including members of Cuban medical teams; long-established bank accounts have been closed; and the costs of bank transfers and the length of time they take have increased. This all creates a need to conduct transactions in cash or through third-country nationals, or to seek alternative methods of payment and procurement, which are often unavailable or entail long delays and reduce the transparency of payments. 97. The United States veto power within universal financial institutions, and threats by the United States to withdraw funding from international institutions that provide financial, technical or other assistance to Cuba in an amount equivalent to the assistance provided, are used with a view to reducing access by Cuba – a developing country that faces high risks of hurricanes and earthquakes – to emergency natural disaster relief funds and assistance, including assistance under projects led and implemented by United Nations entities. 98. The measures in force, despite announced humanitarian exemptions for food and medicine, prevent, impede, delay or make more costly the delivery of the equipment, spare parts and consumables, food, medicine, shelter and clothes necessary to ensure humanitarian relief and the recovery and sustainable development of the population in need, and thus are contrary to the guiding principles for humanitarian assistance set out in the annex to General Assembly resolution 46/182, and to Assembly resolution 58/114, on the strengthening of the coordination of emergency humanitarian assistance of the United Nations. Even where exemptions exist, they do not allow for the delivery of items necessary for the maintenance of critical infrastructure, such as electricity and water supply systems and transportation networks, thus affecting the people of Cuba with regard to their enjoyment of a wide range of human rights. 99. Refusals by producers of medicine, raw materials, medical and agricultural equipment, spare parts, software, vaccines for human beings and livestock, fertilizers and other essential goods to conclude contracts with Cuba, refusals by banks to conduct transactions and refusals by transportation companies to guarantee deliveries have resulted in documented increases in mortality, the worsening of health outcomes and decreased food production, consequently eroding the quality of life of the Cuban people in a way that the Special Rapporteur considers to amount to violations of the rights to food, to the highest attainable standard of health, to live in dignity without pain, and to life. 100. The reported reluctance of foreign partners to cooperate with Cuban educational institutions, sport societies, cultural institutions, artists, athletes and technology and other companies due to the above-mentioned reasons constitutes discrimination on the ground of nationality, affecting the right to education as well as international academic, sports and cultural cooperation, innovation, academic freedoms and cultural rights, including the right of everyone to benefit from the results of scientific progress. 101. The deteriorating economy and the impossibility of guaranteeing employment, decent work and sustainable education, especially for the poorest, have led to increasing migration rates, especially among young people, a reduction in birth rates, high job vacancy rates (up to 50 per cent), especially in the public sector, including the healthcare, education and engineering sectors. 102. Unilateral coercive measures against Cuba have serious extraterritorial effects, impeding the ability of countries that previously benefited from Cuban medical brigades to ensure the highest attainable level of health for their citizens. 103. Existing humanitarian exemptions are ineffective and insufficient, are subject to lengthy and costly procedures and do not cover the delivery of spare parts or equipment and machinery indispensable for the maintenance and restoration of the economy and vital public services. 104. The Special Rapporteur acknowledges the primary responsibility for the promotion and protection of human rights of Cuba and therefore welcomes the efforts of the Government of Cuba to mitigate the negative impact of the United States unilateral sanctions, especially for the most vulnerable persons, and the efforts to ensure access to healthcare, food, education, transportation and emergency assistance across the country.

records.section: V. Assessment of the imposition of sanctions from an international law perspective
records.text: 82. In view of the complexity of unilateral sanctions imposed against Cuba, the current assessment reflects only a few relevant aspects. The Special Rapporteur believes that the national emergency announced by the Government of the United States in 1996 as the grounds for strengthening sanctions against Cuba, and which is still in effect, and the Executive Order 14380, issued by the President of the United States on 29 January 2026, do not meet the requirements set out in article 4 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and further elaborated on in general comment No. 29 (2001) of the Human Rights Committee. Under international law, unilateral measures without or beyond the authorization of the Security Council may be taken only if they do not violate the international obligations of States (that is, they meet the criteria for retortion) or if their wrongfulness can be excluded as countermeasures in accordance with standards of the law of international responsibility. As Cuba and the United States are both States Members of the United Nations and members of the World Trade Organization and are also party to multiple international treaties in different areas of international law, measures taken by the United States cannot be qualified as retortions. 83. Maximum pressure campaigns, threats to third States, companies and individuals, and the initial designation and subsequent re-designations of Cuba as a State sponsor of terrorism run counter to the principle of sovereign equality of States, the prohibition on intervening in the domestic affairs of States, and the principles of peaceful settlement of international disputes and of cooperation in good faith, which constitute peremptory norms of international law. Additionally, no State may exercise jurisdiction over another State as a general principle of law, and therefore no designation as a State sponsor of terrorism is allowed. 84. Although there is no universally recognized customary norm of international law providing for the possibility to enter any port without additional permission, the Special Rapporteur is of the view that the United States prohibition on vessels with any flag entering its ports within 180 days of entering Cuban ports constitutes a violation of the purpose and articles I, II and V of the Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime Traffic, with respect to Cuban vessels, and violations of the same Convention and of relevant bilateral treaties in force for the United States with respect to flag States of other foreign vessels. 85. Applying extraterritorial jurisdiction to nationals and companies of third States for cooperation with Cuban public authorities, nationals and companies, or with reference to the use of the United States dollar for payment, is illegal under international law and increases the risks of overcompliance worldwide. 86. The revocation of the visas of diplomats from third countries and their family members, and/or threats to revoke visas in the future for engaging in agreements on the deployment of Cuban medical teams, has significant extraterritorial effects and constitutes an intervention in the domestic affairs of States around the world that previously benefited from medical assistance provided by Cuban doctors. 87. The Special Rapporteur considers that preventing access to emergency funding and impeding the delivery of humanitarian assistance needed to respond to natural disasters, such as hurricanes, to the dengue and chikungunya epidemics, and to the deepening humanitarian crisis amount to a breach of the guiding principles set out in the annex to General Assembly resolution 46/182, on the strengthening of the coordination of humanitarian emergency assistance of the United Nations, and further developed in subsequent General Assembly resolutions and documents issued by the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs and Inter-Agency Standing Committee documents. 88. Unilateral sanctions against Cuba are not in conformity with a large number of international legal norms, have been introduced to apply pressure on a State and to exclude Cuba from international cooperation and cannot be justified as countermeasures under the law of international responsibility, therefore they are considered to constitute unilateral coercive measures, which have been condemned repeatedly in resolutions of the Human Rights Council and the General Assembly.

records.text: 75. The Government has reportedly adopted a range of strategies aimed at mitigating the social and economic effects of unilateral sanctions against Cuba, focusing on both economic diversification and social protection measures. Central to these efforts is the maintenance of a subsidized basic goods distribution system. According to information received, the current list of subsidized goods includes more than 60 staple food products, such as rice, sugar, vegetable oil, coffee (mixed with fillers), beans, chicken, eggs, salt and bread, as well as certain essential household items, including soap, detergent and pasta. 76. Other essential services, including electricity, water supply, gas and public transportation, are made available at nominal cost. Although these measures aim to provide a minimum level of protection to the population, the Special Rapporteur received consistent reports of shortages of several essential goods and of delays in their distribution across different regions of the country. 77. Social protection policies also include targeted nutritional and dietary support programmes. According to information provided to the Special Rapporteur, specific dietary assistance is available for children and other individuals with particular nutritional or medical needs. These programmes reportedly include additional food allocations for pregnant women, children with chronic illnesses and individuals requiring specialized diets for medical reasons. In particular, children with certain health conditions may receive supplementary products such as fortified milk, specialized nutritional formulas or other dietary support through health and social assistance services. 78. In response to recent natural disasters, additional mitigation measures have reportedly been implemented. The Special Rapporteur was informed that following Hurricane Melissa, reconstruction materials provided to affected populations were subsidized at 50 per cent in order to facilitate the rebuilding of damaged homes and infrastructure. 79. Economic reforms have been introduced in an effort to stimulate domestic production and diversify the economy, including the legalization of micro-, small and medium-sized enterprises (see para. 19 above). These reforms are intended to generate employment opportunities outside the public sector and to support the development of domestic supply chains capable of alleviating shortages of goods and services. 80. In the context of ongoing resource shortages and periodic disruptions affecting electricity, water supply and other critical services, the Government has also established communication mechanisms to inform the population about service interruptions. These channels are used to provide advance notice of scheduled power outages and other service disruptions, allowing households and communities to better anticipate such shortages and manage their impact on daily life. 81. While these mitigation measures demonstrate efforts by the authorities to minimize the effects of the economic hardship on the population, the Special Rapporteur received information indicating that the scale and persistence of supply constraints continue to limit the overall effectiveness of the measures. As a result, many households reportedly remain exposed to shortages of essential goods and services despite the existence of these protective policies.

records.section: E. Access to essential public services and infrastructure
records.text: 68. The functioning of critical infrastructure and maintenance of public services in the country is dependent on imports of equipment, spare parts and relevant materials, including in the spheres of healthcare, education, electricity generation, water distribution, agricultural processing, transportation, telecommunications and the production of pharmaceuticals. 69. Water supply and sanitation services in Cuba are provided through public enterprises. Public water services are provided to approximately 8.4 million people, representing around 85 per cent of the population. The remaining population relies on alternative supply mechanisms, including water trucks and community access points. In some rural areas, these arrangements require individuals to travel 30 minutes or more to collect water. The sewerage network reportedly covers only around 35 per cent of the population, while the remainder relies on septic tanks. 70. Information received indicates that, although a minimum provision of five litres of water per person per day is considered a basic benchmark, current conditions make this target difficult to meet consistently. In Havana, with 2 million inhabitants, authorities have reportedly prioritized energy supply to maintain water services, sometimes at the expense of other sectors. The Special Rapporteur was informed that around 30 water trucks were deployed daily in the city in 2025, a sharp drop from 75 – the number of trucks that had typically been deployed per day previously. Interruptions caused by equipment failures do not necessarily eliminate access to water but do disrupt the distribution cycle, leading to greater reliance on water truck deliveries and lower service quality. Reportedly, while accessibility and water quality have been maintained, the availability of water has deteriorated significantly, with availability levels in some areas reportedly falling below 50 per cent, as compared with system capacity, due in part to limited resources for equipment maintenance. 71. Cuba depends largely on fossil fuels for the production of electricity; only 5 per cent of power generation is from renewable energy sources (hydro, solar and wind). A number of factors, including the disruption of the PetroCaribe system of energy supplies, challenges in delivery, the lack of access to the international credit system, declining exports of Cuban services and goods, the introduction and implementation of the 180-day prohibition on entering the United States ports after vessels enter Cuba, and decreasing tourism, have reduced Cuban foreign currency reserves, thus hampering the country’s ability to purchase fuel, and has affected power plants, rendering the country more exposed to energy shortages. 72. The Special Rapporteur notes that the country’s thermoelectric power stations face significant challenges, due to high levels of decapitalization, as the country lacks access to adequate financial resources to maintain them. One of the country’s largest thermoelectric power plants has reportedly not undergone maintenance for 15 years, despite recommendations for maintenance every five years. Substantial delays in machinery upkeep can increase the likelihood of equipment failures, often irreparably. 73. The cumulative effect of these challenges results in prolonged power outages across large areas of the country, sometimes lasting up to 20 hours per day in certain affected areas. These outages limit access to clean water due to the malfunction of water pumps, disrupt public transportation, affect the preservation of food and impede the provision of a wide range of other essential services. 74. Challenges to importing vehicles and spare parts, the increasing costs of delivery and the insufficient supply of fuel have reduced the capacity of the transportation system; between 2019 and 2024, the number of passengers served dropped by more than 50 per cent. Similar challenges are affecting garbage services, especially in Havana and other large cities.

records.section: D. International cooperation, aid and humanitarian assistance
records.text: 60. Humanitarian operations in Cuba face significant logistical and financial barriers. Restrictions complicate exports and procurement, and humanitarian agencies report severe limitations in scaling up their response due to blocked banks transfers with final beneficiaries in Cuba. Such financial restrictions also can affect United Nations entities, diplomatic missions and humanitarian organizations and individual humanitarian workers. Reports also referred to challenges in the logistics of, and serious delays in, delivery; the risk, or fear, of losing Electronic System for Travel Authorization status simply by working in Cuba that even United Nations international staff, volunteers, donors and other humanitarian actors face; and the unavailability of humanitarian and development financing from the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank and other partners. The Special Rapporteur found this particularly worrisome in a disaster-prone country, where in 2024 alone two hurricanes and two earthquakes occurred within a period of 20 days. Hurricane Melissa struck Cuba immediately before the country visit. 61. The Special Rapporteur notes with particular concern that 2.2 million people in 33 municipalities in the Provinces of Granma, Santiago de Cuba, Holguin and Guantanamo were severely impacted by Hurricane Melissa; housing, basic services and means of communication were critically damaged, and livelihoods and the population’s food security are under threat. Of the population that were critically affected, 50.2 per cent are women and 33.4 per cent live in rural areas, according to the Pan American Health Organization. However, due to the challenges described above, the financing available to Cuba for recovery from Hurricane Melissa is 20 to 25 times lower than that provided for Jamaica, and the number of volunteers assisting in recovery is 35 times lower. 62. Delivery of humanitarian goods is reported to be routed through Jamaica, specifically Kingston, or other alternative routes rather than directly, increasing costs and delays. Financial sanctions affect not only organizations but also individuals, with Cuban residency triggering heightened scrutiny from banks. International humanitarian staff also face personal repercussions, as some lose their Electronic System for Travel Authorization status simply by working in Cuba. These combined obstacles severely limit the ability of humanitarian organizations to deliver timely and effective assistance. 63. According to information received, restrictions on the acquisition of essential supplies and increasing transaction costs have delayed humanitarian operations and severely affected the efficiency of United Nations projects and the implementation of the United Nations cooperation programme in Cuba. Some United Nations entities have been unable to access critical pre-positioned humanitarian items stored in United Nations depots, as some are owned by entities associated with the United States. As a result, time-consuming procurement process are required, leading to higher costs for the United Nations system in the country. 64. Challenges are also reported in the implementation of long-term agreements by United Nations entities, including for the procurement of key office supplies. This undermines the proper functioning of the United Nations entities in Cuba and reportedly even prevented the donation of computers to a school, thus affecting the right to education and United Nations development projects. 65. United Nations entities in Cuba are effectively restricted from maintaining corporate accounts with United States financial institutions or conducting transactions in United States dollars. All payment processing requires exhaustive compliance verification with the United States Office of Foreign Assets Control. Transactions reportedly require conversion to non dollar currencies and routing through intermediary banks, delaying implementation by several months. United Nations staff in Cuba face restrictions in their personal banking, including restrictions on using Cuban accounts for travel-related transactions, and complex visa requirements for official travel, which affects regional coordination. 66. Humanitarian and development financing from the World Bank, the Inter American Development Bank and other partners is restricted when Cuba is involved, and even long term agreements are sometimes disregarded. 67. Deliveries of humanitarian goods are severely affected by zero-risk policies and overcompliance on the part of States, banks, donors, private companies and even United Nations entities. As a result, procurement for humanitarian and development projects is difficult to ensure and is often cancelled at the last minute, resulting in increased costs and deferring prolonged delays in the delivery of aid.

records.section: C. Education, academic cooperation and access to information
records.text: 48. Education remains a cornerstone of Cuban social policy. During her visit, the Special Rapporteur observed the central role that education continues to play in the country’s development strategy. Cuba allocates a significant share of public resources to education, dedicating approximately 7 per cent of its gross domestic product – representing more than 20 per cent of the State budget – to primary, secondary and tertiary education. The country reports a literacy rate of 99.8 per cent. 49. Despite these achievements, the Special Rapporteur received information indicating that the realization of the right to education is affected by shortages of books and educational materials. These shortages are attributed, in part, to high shipping costs and delays in the importation of supplies. According to information provided to the Special Rapporteur, the country’s three main printing facilities have reduced their operations due to shortages of paper and ink, and have prioritized the printing of newspapers and official publications. As a result, materials associated with the III Perfeccionamiento initiative (the curriculum reform, covering all levels of education, implemented between 2024 and 2025) had not yet been printed as at the time of the visit. Fuel shortages and limited transportation capacity have further delayed the distribution of educational materials, particularly in remote areas, thereby exacerbating regional disparities in access to learning resources. 50. In addition, technological obsolescence reportedly affects the functioning of the education system. At the time of the visit, it was estimated that only around 55 per cent of the computers installed in educational institutions were functional. Such constraints affect both the quality of teaching and the capacity of institutions to incorporate new technologies into learning processes. 51. Beyond material constraints affecting the education system itself, testimonies received by the Special Rapporteur indicate that Cuban academics and educational institutions face growing obstacles in engaging in international academic cooperation. Several stakeholders reported that there was increasing reluctance among foreign partners to collaborate with Cuban institutions. Reported challenges include difficulties transferring funds for academic projects and scholarships, obstacles in obtaining visas for Cuban scholars and limitations on opening bank accounts abroad to receive scholarship funds. According to testimonies received, these challenges contribute to the progressive isolation of Cuban academic and research communities from international networks. For example, two Cuban scholars who travelled to the Dominican Republic for professional purposes were reportedly denied hotel bookings due to the policies of a United States company prohibiting the provision of services to Cuban nationals. 52. Restrictions affecting access to digital tools and information were also reported to have implications for scientific and academic development. Reference was made to the United States Presidential Memorandum No. 5 of 2017, which reportedly resulted in the geoblocking of more than 320 Internet pages and resources in Cuba. The affected services include open-information repositories, virtual laboratories, artificial intelligence platforms, cloud-based services, mapping tools and coding environments commonly used in academic and research activities. Even where websites are not geoblocked, slow Internet connections and outdated technological infrastructure reportedly prevent users from loading or accessing many online resources. 53. Cuban academics, scholars and researchers continue to publish in international scientific journals; however, their ability to travel abroad to attend international conferences and academic exchanges has been hampered by difficulties related to flight availability, visa issuance and financial transfers. Reportedly, many publishing houses have refused to deliver author copies to Cuban scholars. One testimony concerned a Cuban scholar residing in Spain who had faced significant obstacles in opening a bank account because of her Cuban nationality. 54. Information was also received regarding the organization of a scientific university congress scheduled to be held in Cuba in February 2026; some third country researchers expressed concern that their participation in the Congress could lead to restrictions on their future entry into the United States, where some maintain ongoing academic projects and family ties. 55. Additional constraints affect access to research equipment and technological resources. In some cases, Cuban institutions must purchase entirely new equipment in hard currency, often at prices estimated to be 35 to 40 per cent above market rates, without certainty that spare parts or software support will remain available in the future. Cuban institutions and individuals have also reportedly resorted to barter arrangements as an alternative means of obtaining equipment essential for scientific development and the right to access information. Despite the existence of general licences and exemptions that authorize travel and transactions related to educational activities, including academic exchanges, study abroad programmes and participation in Internet-based courses involving Cuban nationals, information received indicates that these provisions are often not effectively applied in practice. According to testimonies received, these factors have further compromised the ability of Cuban nationals to fully exercise their right to education, to participate in international academic exchange and cooperation and to benefit from the results of scholarly research. 56. The availability of assistive tools for students with disabilities has also reportedly declined. Information received indicates that at least 538 wheelchairs, as well as adapted classroom furniture, are currently needed for students with special educational needs. The Special Rapporteur was informed, for example, that 39 of the 259 children who have received cochlear implants require replacement procedures that cannot currently be carried out due to the lack of the necessary medical equipment. Similarly, the number of functioning printers used for Braille writing has reportedly declined significantly: of the original 20 devices available in the country, only 3 remain operational, as the others cannot be repaired due to the lack of spare parts. These shortages limit the ability of educational institutions to ensure inclusive learning environments for students with disabilities. 57. Similar challenges were reported regarding the provision of extracurricular activities for children, including sports, music, dancing and art, which is hindered by fuel shortages and the unreliability of public transportation. 58. The Special Rapporteur also received information indicating that the sports sector is affected by sanctions-related constraints. Among the issues raised was the difficulty in processing membership payments to certain international sports organizations. For example, in 2025 Cuba reportedly attempted to make a payment to the World Anti-Doping Agency. Although the payment was initiated, the Central Bank of Cuba was reportedly informed that the transaction had been returned in accordance with the internal policy of the beneficiary bank. This led to delays in the payment, which at the time of writing has not been completed, and may prevent Cuba from participating in certain international competitions until payment is successfully processed. 59. Testimonies from high-level athletes alleged that some international sports brands refrain from sponsoring Cuban athletes due to concerns related to sanctions and, in some cases, may overcomply with related restrictions, thus limiting athletes’ opportunities to secure sponsorship and representation agreements. Athletes also reported concerns about potential last-minute restrictions affecting their participation in international competitions, increases in travel costs due to last-minute procurement; challenges with regard to currency exchange in the country of competition; difficulties in procuring necessary sport equipment; and difficulties in receiving awards they have won. In addition, it was reported that certain advanced sports technologies are available only in the United States and are therefore inaccessible to Cuban athletes.

records.text: 38. Although medicines and medical equipment are technically exempted from sanctions, access to health is reported to be severely affected by the 10 per cent de minimis rule, including through the expanded applicability of the rule as a result of acquisitions of foreign companies by United States persons and companies, as well as by challenges in delivering cargo, all of which increase costs substantially. This has resulted in the widespread inaccessibility of a significant number of medicines in Cuba, including medicine to treat cancer and heart disease, as well as of insect repellents and tests for dengue and other infections. It has also resulted in the inaccessibility of equipment, spare parts, reagents, consumables and raw materials, undermining the development of medicine and vaccines in Cuba and making domestic testing impossible. The purchase of replacement parts for machinery through third parties may be authorized through special licences from the United States Office of Foreign Assets Control; such licences reportedly take 6 to 12 months to obtain. Occasionally, when spare parts are unavailable, hospitals and clinics are compelled to reinstall entire machines, resulting in unforeseen and additional expenditures. 39. The Special Rapporteur notes the example of a high-technology German encapsulation machine that reportedly broke down in 2023; the machine’s manufacturer, Harro Höfliger, subsequently stated it would cease supplying Cuba with parts and technical assistance until further notice. During her visit, the Special Rapporteur reviewed specific exchanges between health technology providers in Germany working with encapsulating machines and Cuban pharmaceutical companies, in which the providers indicated that they were unable to send their technical personnel to Cuba due to the impact of the sanctions imposed by the United States. Attempts to hire subcontractors to repair essential machinery reportedly did not succeed. In other cases, owing to the reluctance of other nationals to travel to Cuba, technology providers based in Europe reportedly had to deploy Russian technicians to carry out the necessary maintenance and repairs. In practice, this has prevented Cuban pharmaceutical companies from producing or encapsulating medicines, including gastro protective drugs and fluconazole. 40. According to information received, there are currently 96,000 patients on the waiting list for surgery. Of these, around 11,000 are children. Over 4,507 cancer patients are unable to undergo the surgeries they are waiting for, due to a lack of specialized machinery. Other critical medical equipment, including machines for the detection of colorectal cancer, are also unavailable in Cuba, which has substantially limited cancer-screening programmes. 41. The Special Rapporteur further notes that, even when dealing with non-United States suppliers, special licences from the United States Office of Foreign Assets Control are required for the import of some medicines, including those produced by companies such as Pfizer, creating additional delays in access to essential medical treatments and an undeniable deterrent effect among pharmaceutical companies. 42. Similar challenges have been reported as regards diagnostics, disease prevention and treatment. In particular, in 2023, United Nations entities were “advised” not to accept dengue tests donated by China, despite the dengue outbreak. During her visit, the Special Rapporteur was also informed about serious shortages of paracetamol and insect repellent, which were essential during the chikungunya outbreak in the country. 43. The application of the 10 per cent de minimis rule is also reportedly undermining the development of vaccines. During her visit, the Special Rapporteur was informed that the only equipment on the market to ensure the compliance of vaccines with international quality control standards is manufactured by a United States company, while the equipment that Cuba possesses is currently out of service due to the country’s inability to purchase necessary spare parts. This is particularly critical as Cuba was one of the few countries that developed its own coronavirus disease (COVID-19) vaccine (Soberana), and the first in Latin America to do so. The impossibility of testing vaccines therefore has a transborder effect, affecting the right to health not only in Cuba, but in the whole region. 44. In addition, the Special Rapporteur is concerned about the reported severe challenges faced in ensuring that the healthcare needs of vulnerable groups are met, including through the provision of baby formula, transplants for those who need them, and sanitary pads for women and girls. Glasses and hearing devices for older persons are repaired domestically where resources are available; that is often not sufficient. 45. Additionally, since August 2025, the United States has revoked the visas of a number of State officials, and their family members, from countries that had benefited from medical teams deployed abroad to underserved regions under the medical cooperation programme of Cuba. Teams have reportedly operated in more than 165 countries since the creation of the programme in 1960. Some foreign officials even faced challenges in participating in Pan American Health Organization meetings as a result, which affected international cooperation in healthcare. 46. During her visit, the Special Rapporteur received information that, since 2021, diplomatic staff in embassies who had facilitated the arrival of Cuban medical brigades in African and Caribbean countries have had their approval under the Electronic System for Travel Authorization revoked. Reportedly, aid from the United States to those countries has been conditioned on the gradual withdrawal from the medical cooperation programme implemented by Cuba. Such measures affect the labour rights of Cuban medical doctors, decrease possibilities for exchange, reduce external income for Cubans and have severe extraterritorial effects on the right to health and to life in underserved communities and in situations of emergency abroad. The Special Rapporteur is concerned to note that, since her visit took place, several countries have decided to end participation in the Cuban medical cooperation programme, allegedly due to pressure from the United States. 47. The Special Rapporteur also heard testimonies from students at the Latin American School of Medicine, most of whom receive scholarships from the Government of Cuba, on the lack of access to advanced medical technology; they also noted that access to many sources of information is blocked in the country. In addition, the School has faced obstacles in paying administrative fees to the Union of Universities of Latin America and the Caribbean, owing to the repeated rejection of financial transactions; this affects the right to education and the right to health extraterritorially.

records.text: 31. Food security in the country is reportedly severely impacted by a lack of fuel and the limited possibilities for importing food, seeds, fertilizer, livestock vaccines and equipment and spare parts for food production, processing, conservation and delivery. According to information received, the food industry has observed a noticeable decrease in production; it was estimated that production capacity, which was at 32 per cent in 2023, would drop to 22 per cent by the end of 2025. Also according to information received, the country reported a 21 per cent drop in beef production between 2023 and 2024. As of 2025, Cuba was operating with only 40 per cent of the fuel required for irrigation pumps, tractors and agricultural product transportation. 32. For this reason, the Government promoted municipal self-sufficiency through the Food Sovereignty and Nutritional Security Law (Law No. 148/2022), encouraging the growth of small livestock farming (pigs, poultry, fish and rabbits), but this failed to meet the target of 5 kg of meat per person per month. Poultry production remained low due to feed shortages. As of January 2024, the annual inflation rate for food items was officially estimated at 37.2 per cent, down from the rate of approximately 70 per cent estimated the previous year, but still a very high level. 33. Due to declining agricultural output, the food industry in Cuba has increasingly relied on imports of raw materials – 70 to 80 per cent of its food. Since 2021, when Cuba was re designated as a State sponsor of terrorism, there has also been a reported decrease in the number of imports of food items such as powdered milk, flour, poultry, beef and pork. In the case of wheat, Cuba was only able to meet 67 per cent of its needs in 2023 – 38 per cent less than in 2022. 34. Poultry imported from the United States is reportedly the main source of animal protein consumed in Cuba. However, when procurement from the United States, is possible, payment must be made 45 days in advance, in cash, in United States dollars and suppliers must possess a United States Office of Foreign Assets Control licence. The Bureau of Industry and Security of the United States will generally deny applications to export or re export items for use by entities on the List of Entities and Subentities Associated with Cuba. All of the above creates substantial obstacles in a country where the availability of cash is limited. As a result, imports are frequently conducted through intermediary suppliers, which can increase costs by around 35 per cent due to reduced profit margins and additional commissions. Reportedly, financing or credit arrangements are not available, affecting rations and, consequently, reducing the number of meals people are able to eat daily. 35. Impediments to securing sufficient milk for children’s rations have also been reported. While the World Food Programme provided assistance to ensure the delivery of more than 350 tons of powdered milk, the delivery met less than 20 per cent of the country’s estimated monthly needs (1,800 tons). As delivery companies often fear entering Cuban ports, delivery delays can reportedly reach up to six months. 36. Due to restrictions on the use of United States dollars in transactions, Cuban agricultural companies reportedly must be invoiced in euros or other foreign currencies, based on the exchange rate applicable on the date of billing. When the payment is ultimately processed, banks apply the exchange rate in effect on the date of payment, which may generate additional costs due to currency fluctuations. 37. The Special Rapporteur is concerned about the critical situation with regard to food insecurity in the country. In particular, in around 70 per cent of Cuban households at least one member eats less or skips meals; in around the same percentage of households, at least one member runs out of food due to a lack of cash or the inability to access cash. Prolonged shortages of fresh food, such as poultry, eggs and vegetables, are one of the main causes of undernourishment, with the subsidized food products offered by the ration card (la libreta) covering only around 40 per cent of the recommended energy intake.

records.section: III. Impact of unilateral coercive measures on the economy
records.text: 20. Due to the severe limitations on international trade, the international trade balance of Cuba continues to reflect a deficit. In 2024, exports from Cuba were valued at US$ 2.128 billion, while the trade deficit was assessed at approximately US$ 5.368 billion. The currency system in Cuba functions as a multilayered, partially dollarized economy using three different exchange rates. The current uncertainty around the national currency is reflected in regular devaluations, which affect the prices of basic commodities and feed speculation, thus leading to further uncertainty; all of this has a negative impact on people’s lives. The average salary in the public sector is reportedly low; in 2025, it amounted to 6,649 Cuban pesos per month. 21. The Special Rapporteur notes that although remittances are formally exempt from United States unilateral sanctions, in practice, they became difficult – or almost impossible – to receive after the withdrawal of various remittance services, such as Western Union, from the country early in 2025. 22. According to information the Special Rapporteur received, tourism, which represents the highest amount of revenue for the Cuban economy and constitutes approximately 10 per cent of the country’s gross domestic product, has been severely affected by the designation of Cuba as a State sponsor of terrorism and the intensification of sanctions since 2016. United States tourism agencies and hotel groups have withdrawn from the country, while travel restrictions, limitations on credit card payments and widespread overcompliance have seriously compromised any efforts to revitalize this critical sector of the economy. For example, she received information indicating that the number of cruise ship stopovers at Cuban ports has fallen by over 90 per cent since 2016. 23. Significant emigration is another factor significantly affecting the Cuban economy. The peak was reported in 2022, when over 300,000 Cubans emigrated to the United States, Europe and Latin America. Multiple and diverse actors reported significant brain drain in the country, which had resulted in the loss of human capital in all professions and sectors, including those that provide basic services to the population. 24. Deliveries to Cuba for which a United States Office of Foreign Assets Control licence has not been obtained entail much higher costs (reportedly 40 to 300 per cent higher) owing to: the 10 per cent de minimis rule concerning United States content in products and United States patents; the need to operate through several intermediary companies and banks; the much longer delivery routes (largely from Asia and Europe); the inability of exporters to participate in trade on a competitive basis; intermediary tariffs; premiums added by suppliers to compensate for their own risk of exposure to sanctions; extensive de-risking and overcompliance by suppliers, transportation and insurance companies due to the possible exclusion from the United States market; and risks of high fines, especially in the banking sector. 25. Entrepreneurs also reported significant limitations in accessing digital services and technological platforms. Accounts on collaboration and cloud-based services have reportedly been suspended when associated with Cuban IP addresses, while access to major technology providers is restricted due to their links to the United States or concerns about sanctions compliance. As a result, Cuban entrepreneurs often rely on indirect or informal solutions, including the use of third parties or personal networks, to obtain necessary tools and equipment. 26. Testimonies further indicated that restrictions on technology and supply chains resulted in increased costs. Goods and technological equipment are often purchased through intermediaries, which may increase prices by an estimated 30 to 40 per cent above the retail value. In some cases, essential items must be brought into the country through personal travel. 27. Entrepreneurs also spoke of the legal uncertainty in their commercial relations with international clients. Some entrepreneurs indicated that, because certain transactions involving Cuban entities may be considered prohibited under sanctions regimes, entrepreneurs lack effective legal remedies if foreign clients fail to honour contractual obligations or payments. 28. Given the unpredictability of United States sanctions, their expansion over the last decade and the risks that a change in the United States administration, and the resulting approach toward the country, may entail, even if sanctions were to be relieved, foreign companies are likely hesitant to make substantial investments in the country, particularly with regard to infrastructure and local entrepreneurs. 29. As a result, the Government of Cuba, private entities and citizens are hampered from engaging in long term planning, which forces social and political initiatives to remain short term, due to the precarious situation, rife with sudden cancellations, backpedalling and unpredictability.

records.text: 7. For over six decades, the United States of America has maintained a wide-ranging regime of economic, trade and financial sanctions against Cuba, marking the longest-standing sanctions policy in the history of United States foreign relations. Entire generations of Cubans have lived under the constraints of this financial and economic sanctions regime, which has shaped the country’s economic and social landscape. 8. The sanctions regime was imposed in 1962, and formalized with the issuance of the Cuban Assets Control Regulations, which prohibited all trade and financial transactions with Cuba except for those specifically authorized by the United States Office of Foreign Assets Control, which operates under the Department of the Treasury. This regulatory framework built upon earlier legislative frameworks, including the Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917 and the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. Over subsequent decades, the sanctions regime was further reinforced and expanded through additional legal instruments: the Export Administration Regulations of 1979, the Cuban Democracy Act of 1992 (also known as the Torricelli Act) and the Helms-Burton Act of 1996. The Helms-Burton Act codified the embargo and extended its extraterritorial reach by imposing penalties on foreign companies, and their executives, engaged in transactions involving United States property nationalized in Cuba, while also enabling legal action against Cuba in domestic courts in the United States. 9. The United States Department of State first designated Cuba as a State sponsor of terrorism in 1982, citing alleged support for international terrorist organizations operating in Latin America. This designation remained in effect for over 30 years, until 2015, when Cuba was removed from the State sponsor of terrorism list following an October 2014 policy directive aimed at normalizing bilateral relations. According to information received during the visit, the effects of this normalization were felt widely in various sectors in Cuba, including through the admission of United States airlines, cruise lines and businesses, which in turn improved the livelihoods of workers, particularly those in coastal areas, and significantly facilitated the sending of remittances, among other benefits. 10. In addition, certain restrictions were eased, including financial restrictions and restrictions on the travel of United States citizens to Cuba, including for education. These policies were reversed and restrictions tightened in 2016 and, in January 2021, Cuba was re designated as a State sponsor of terrorism for allegedly harbouring fugitives who committed or supported acts of terrorism in the United States and for refusing to extradite to Colombia several leaders of the Ejército de Liberación Nacional for their alleged involvement in a terrorist attack in Bogotá in 2019. 11. The United States Trade Sanctions Reform and Export Enhancement Act of 2000 allows for the direct, cash-based export of agricultural commodities, medicine and medical devices from the United States to specific sanctioned countries, including Cuba, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, Iran (Islamic Republic of) and the Sudan. A key feature of the Act is that it required the President of the United States to terminate unilateral sanctions on agricultural or medical products that were in place at the time of the enactment of the Act, unless the products were on the United States Munitions List, on specific control lists or linked to chemical, biological and other weapons. It also grants the Congress of the United States the ability to veto future presidential proposals to impose unilateral sanctions on the items for which export is authorized under the Act. The export of agricultural products to Cuba is authorized on the condition that payment is made in cash, in advance and without United States financing. Travel to Cuba by United States persons for tourist activities is prohibited, with tourist activity defined as any activity involving travel to, from or within Cuba that was not explicitly authorized under title 31, section 515.560, of the Code of Federal Regulations. 12. Early in 2025, the United States Department of State announced the reinstatement of the List of Entities and Subentities Associated with Cuba (often referred to as the Cuba Restricted List), which restricts transactions with government-linked Cuban entities. The original list had been created during the Administration of President Donald J. Trump in 2017 and had been rescinded during the Administration of President Joseph Biden in January 2025. On 7 February 2025, 237 entities were added to the List, including ministries, holding companies, hotels, tourist agencies, marinas, stores and entities serving the defence and security sectors. 13. Under the 10 per cent de minimis rule established in the Export Administration Regulations, the amount of United States-origin content in goods exported to Cuba is limited to a maximum of 10 per cent by value. Consequently, if a foreign-made product contains more than 10 per cent United States-origin content, it may be subject to the Export Administration Regulations if exported to Cuba from another country. 14. In the Cuban Democracy Act, the subsidiaries of United States companies in third countries were prohibited from trading goods with Cuba or with Cuban nationals. This Act codified the 180-day rule, which establishes that vessels that have visited a Cuban port to engage in trade are prohibited for 180 days from entering a United States port to load or unload freight, unless specifically authorized by the United States Department of the Treasure. 15. The Trade Sanctions Reform and Export Enhancement Act of 2000 stipulates that Cuba is to pay for United States imports in full and in advance, which is increasingly difficult due to limited Cuban access to foreign currency. The Act allows the export of medical equipment and medicines to Cuba subject to regulatory licensing; however, United States suppliers are reportedly not interested, due to overcompliance. 16. The Special Rapporteur notes the existence of licences for, among other things, family remittances, humanitarian donations and telecommunications-related operations, as well as Support for the Cuban People licences, for travel and the provision of services and supplies to the private sector, created by the Department of the Treasury during the diplomatic thaw of 2014–2016. Exports of information technology and equipment that promote connectivity and communication are also permitted, provided they do not involve direct investment in State infrastructure. 17. As a result of the enforcement of the United States unilateral sanctions against Cuba and other States, several major international banks have faced heavy fines. In particular, BNP Paribas paid a record US$ 8.9 billion in 2014 through a settlement, while UniCredit agreed to pay a settlement of US$ 611 million in 2019. Smaller penalties were imposed on a subsidiary of Credit Agricole Corporate and Investment Bank, which settled for US$ 401,000 in 2022, and EFG International agreed to pay over US$ 3.5 million in 2024. Testimonies received by the Special Rapporteur during the visit confirm that, given the potentially high cost of penalties, businesses and suppliers engage in overcompliance, going beyond the legal requirements of the applicable sanctions framework. 18. After the United States military intervention in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela on 3 January 2026 and the subsequent cessation of shipments of Venezuelan oil supplies to Cuba, the supply of crude and refined oil products to the island has been sharply curtailed, contributing to a critical fuel shortage. This shortage, compounded by existing structural and infrastructural challenges, which are covered in the present report, has exacerbated electricity outages, constrained essential services and deepened the broader economic difficulties facing the population. On 29 January 2026, President Trump issued Executive Order 14380, declaring a purported national emergency and authorizing the imposition of trade tariffs on imports from third countries who provide oil to Cuba, establishing a de facto oil embargo against Cuba. 19. In 2021, to mitigate the negative effects of the abovementioned measures, the Government of Cuba adopted a comprehensive and multisectoral economic and social government programme. Under the programme, the Government legalized micro-, small and medium-sized enterprises, in order to stimulate domestic production and generate employment outside the public sector, which currently accounts for 35 per cent of total employment. The Special Rapporteur had the opportunity to meet with representatives of some of the enterprises during her visit. They informed her that they must receive payments through third-party intermediaries in other countries, such as Canada or Spain, rather than directly in Cuba.

records.text: 33. In the light of its general recommendation No. 31 (2005) on the prevention of racial discrimination in the administration and functioning of the criminal justice system, the Committee reminds the State Party that the absence or small number of complaints or legal actions brought by victims of racial discrimination may reveal that there is a lack of specific relevant legislation, that victims have inadequate information concerning their rights, that they fear social censure, reprisals or the cost and complexity of the judicial process, that there is a lack of trust in the police and judicial authorities or that the authorities are insufficiently alert to or aware of offences involving racism. Taking into account its previous concluding observations, the Committee urges the State Party to: (a) Ensure that the legal framework for combating racial discrimination contains appropriate provisions, facilitate the reporting of cases and guarantee access for all victims to effective and impartial judicial and non-judicial remedies and adequate reparations; (b) Revise the aforementioned protocols to make them more effective and ensure that the use of administrative fines for offences of discrimination is fully compatible with the Convention and does not impede access to effective judicial protection; (c) Run campaigns to inform the general public, in particular the groups most vulnerable to racial discrimination, of the rights enshrined in the Convention and the mechanisms and remedies available to them to exercise these rights; (d) Step up its efforts to ensure that victims of racial discrimination have effective access to free legal aid services and allocate sufficient human and financial resources to these services; (e) Strengthen the training delivered to public officials, prosecutors, judges, magistrates and law enforcement officials so that they are able to effectively handle cases of racial discrimination, and establish independent evaluation mechanisms to assess whether such cases are being underreported; (f) Collect statistics on complaints of racial discrimination and racially motivated offences, disaggregated by the ethnic or national origin of the victims and other relevant variables related to intersectional discrimination, and on the prosecution and conviction of the perpetrators and the reparations awarded to the victims.

records.section: Discrimination against people of African descent
records.text: 19. Bearing in mind its previous concluding observations, and in the light of its general recommendations No. 31 (2005) on the prevention of racial discrimination in the administration and functioning of the criminal justice system, No. 32 (2009) on the meaning and scope of special measures in the Convention and No. 34 (2011) on racial discrimination against people of African descent, the Committee recommends that the State Party intensify its efforts to adopt and effectively implement, at all levels of government, the special measures or affirmative action necessary to eliminate the structural discrimination and inequality faced by people of African descent, ensuring their broad and inclusive participation in the design, implementation and evaluation of these measures. The Committee also recommends that the State Party: (a) Step up efforts to improve the living conditions of people of African descent by guaranteeing their protection against discrimination by State bodies and public officials or by any individual, group or organization; (b) Take concrete measures to reduce the poverty, vulnerability and marginalization that disproportionately affect people of African descent and to eliminate the obstacles that prevent this group from effectively enjoying their economic, social and cultural rights; (c) Strengthen efforts to prevent and combat racial discrimination in the workplace and improve the access of people of African descent to the formal economy, skilled jobs and management positions; (d) Conduct a thorough analysis of the reasons for the overrepresentation of people of African descent in prisons, with a view to effectively addressing the underlying factors, and collect data, disaggregated by ethnic origin, skin colour and other relevant factors, as a matter of routine at all stages of criminal proceedings.

While the Committee takes note of the explanations provided by the State Party, it is concerned that the Criminal Code does not fully cover all the grounds of discrimination mentioned in article 1 of the Convention, such as descent, and does not cover all the obligations assumed by the State Party under article 4, including the provisions prohibiting public authorities and institutions from promoting or inciting racial discrimination and prohibiting assistance to racist activities, including the financing thereof. records.text: 27. The Committee notes that the State party has strengthened its normative framework to protect women from gender-based violence, including by criminalizing “the death of a woman for gender-based reasons” in the Penal Code and enacting the Comprehensive Strategy for the Prevention of and Attention to Gender Violence and Violence in the Family. It is concerned, however, about the high prevalence of gender-based violence against women and girls in the State party. In particular, the Committee notes with concern: (a) The high number of femicides, cases of rape, assault and other sexual crimes, as well as cases of domestic violence, particularly against women and girls of African descent; (b) The lack of government shelters for victims of gender-based violence, in particular domestic violence, including those accompanied by their children; (c) The lack of comprehensive legislation criminalizing all forms of gender-based violence against women, covering both the public and private spheres; (d) The high level of gender-based violence and police brutality against lesbian, bisexual, transgender and intersex women, including women of African descent, as well as their stigmatization, lack of protection and the low prosecution and conviction rates in such cases.

In line with the Committee’s general recommendation No. 40 (2024) on the equal and inclusive representation of women in decision-making systems, the participation of women in civil society, especially in women’s rights organizations, is essential for ensuring the equal and inclusive representation of women in decision-making systems, including in the development of gender-responsive legislation and policies. The Committee urges the State party to: (a) Repeal the Law on Associations to allow for the establishment of independent women’s associations, including non-governmental organizations; (b) Refrain from using provisions of the Penal Code to unduly restrict the legitimate work of women activists and independent non-governmental organizations; (c) Protect women’s civil society organizations, women human rights defenders and women activists from all forms of reprisals and create an enabling environment for them to carry out their legitimate work freely.

records.text: 8. The Committee recognizes the efforts made by the State party to protect and promote women’s human rights and advance gender equality. It notes with concern, however, the socioeconomic impact of the sanctions imposed by the United States of America on the State party over the past 60 years, recognized by the General Assembly in its resolutions on the necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba (see e.g. Assembly resolution 77/7), and the State party’s redesignation as a State sponsor of terrorism in 2021, which have exacerbated the deterioration of the national economy. In particular, the Committee notes with concern that the State party currently suffers from shortages of food, medicines, medical supplies, fuel and construction materials and that it has intermittent access to electricity, which have a disproportionate impact on women and girls. This has also resulted in large-scale migration of over 1 million persons aged 15–59. It notes that the situation has been intensified by prolonged blackouts, which have further limited access to healthcare, education, food, hygiene, transportation and other basic services for women, girls and the population in general. In addition, the Committee is concerned at the extreme responses by the State party to persons participating in street protests in relation to these circumstances and the resulting reprisals and detentions, especially since the 2019 protests.

records.text: 7. The Committee stresses the crucial role of the legislative power in ensuring the full implementation of the Convention (see A/65/38 , part two, annex VI). The Committee welcomes the international support for the Sustainable Development Goals and calls for the realization of de jure (legal) and de facto (substantive) gender equality, in accordance with the provisions of the Convention, throughout the process of implementing the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The Committee recalls the importance of Goal 5 and of the mainstreaming of the principles of equality and non-discrimination throughout all 17 Goals. It urges the State party to recognize women as the driving force of the sustainable development of Cuba and to adopt relevant policies and strategies to that effect.

records.text: 55. The Committee invites the State party to submit its combined seventh and eighth periodic reports by 19 September 2027 and to include therein information on the follow-up to the present concluding observations. The report should be in compliance with the Committee’s harmonized treaty-specific reporting guidelines and should not exceed 21,200 words. In the event that a report exceeding the established word limit is submitted, the State party will be asked to shorten the report. If the State party is not in a position to review and resubmit the report, translation thereof for the purposes of consideration by the treaty body cannot be guaranteed.

records.section: B. National mechanism for reporting and follow-up
records.text: 54. The Committee recommends that the State party strengthen its national mechanism for reporting and follow-up and ensure that it has the mandate and the adequate human, technical and financial resources to effectively coordinate and prepare reports to international and regional human rights mechanisms and to coordinate and track national follow-up to, and implementation of, treaty obligations and the recommendations and decisions emanating from such mechanisms. The Committee emphasizes that such a structure should be adequately and continuously supported by dedicated staff and should have the capacity to consult systematically with civil society.

records.text: 50. The Committee regrets the lack of information on the implementation of its concluding observations on the State party’s report under the Optional Protocol on the involvement of children in armed conflict. Recalling its previous concluding observations on the report of the State party submitted under article 8 of the Optional Protocol, the Committee recommends that the State party: (a) Set 18 years as the minimum age for voluntary recruitment into the armed forces; (b) Prohibit and criminalize the recruitment and use of children under the age of 18 in hostilities by armed forces, non-State armed groups and security companies; (c) Define and punish the recruitment of children under the age of 15 as a war crime; (d) Define the minimum age for participating in hostilities as 18, including in times of national emergency; (e) Ban military-type training, including the use of firearms, for children under the age of 18, and ensure that any military school for children takes into account human rights principles; (f) Ensure that child members of the Production and Defence Brigades are prohibited effectively from participating in hostilities in cases of national emergency.
